topic.title: The seat lottery home
topic.claim: Every city runs on people who go home twice a year, and for them the station isn't a journey, it's a holding pen.
topic.behaviour: Workers from Delhi heading to Bihar and UP for Chhath wait in holding areas, and platform entry is limited to people with confirmed tickets. The system plans for the rush like it is an emergency, even though it comes every year.
topic.mechanism: Trains are added late and temporary fixes get reused each season. A rush that happens on the same dates every year is still managed like a surprise.
topic.group: Migrant workers and their friends in metros, who go home only for the big festivals
topic.moment: You open the ticket app at 8 am the day booking opens, and every train home already shows a waiting list.

turn.believed: Festival crowds are a one-time rush that the railways handle as best they can.
turn.actually: The rush is on the calendar every year, and the fix is still a waiting area outside the platform.

topic.feeling: Taken for granted by the city I work for
topic.villain: A transport system that handles a predictable annual rush with temporary arrangements
topic.because: Adding permanent capacity for two peak weeks is expensive, so crowd control is cheaper than seats. The people who bear the cost have no way to push back.

proof.fact: Platform tickets are suspended from 3 to 14 November at six Delhi stations, and a permanent holding area outside Platform 16 at New Delhi can hold about 7,000 people.

topic.payoff: The city counts on you to leave on those dates, and it still isn't ready when you do.
topic.send_to: A colleague who is leaving for Chhath and has no confirmed seat
real_details: A second holding area was commissioned at Anand Vihar Terminal this year
topic.news_peg: Platform tickets suspended at six Delhi stations from 3 to 14 November (2026-11-03) and Chhath holding areas (2026-11-09)
topic.why_now: Chhath travel is happening right now.

score.why: The waiting list and the holding pen for the trip home are lived by millions every Diwali and Chhath. The turn is that the city counts on you leaving and still isn't ready.
